text: Akeldama Cave 1, in the lower Ben Hinnom valley at the foot of the west bank of the Kidron valley, east of the convent of St. Onuphrius. A rock-cut burial cave of four chambers: an entrance chamber, two burial chambers with loculi (kokhim), and a back chamber with three arcosolia and burial troughs. A rock-cut courtyard, shared with Cave 2, lies in front of the cave. The entrance (0.6 x 0.6 m) is cut in the center of the courtyard's southwest wall and was found closed by its square sealing stone in situ. Loculi were sealed with stone slabs; a broken stone door with pivoting hinges lay in the entrance chamber. Two shorter loculi were probably used as bone repositories. The burial troughs were covered with stone slabs; letters of the Hebrew alphabet were drawn in charcoal on the slabs of one trough. Eight ossuaries with collected bones. The report dates the tomb's original burials to the first century CE, possibly from the first century BCE, with cremation burials of the Late Roman period and coffin burials of the fifth to seventh centuries CE.

text: Akeldama Cave 2, in the lower Ben Hinnom valley at the foot of the west bank of the Kidron valley, beside Cave 1. A rock-cut burial cave of three chambers: a main chamber with ten loculi (kokhim), a lower repository chamber for ossuaries, and a lower burial chamber with loculi and three arcosolia, one with a burial trough covered by stone slabs. It was entered from the courtyard shared with Cave 1. The entrance (0.6 x 0.6 m) faced northwest and was found closed by a square blocking stone. Several loculus sealing slabs had been removed in antiquity. The back chamber was closed by a hinged stone door with an iron lock. Sixteen ossuaries and a decorated sarcophagus. Ossuary inscriptions, mostly Greek, give the names Kyria, Chares, Eiras, Erota, Jesua, Megiste, and Hermione and Eros, children of Doras; one ossuary bears the artist's name, Aza[ria] son of Berous; the sarcophagus bears a Greek inscription. The report dates the tomb's original burials to the first century CE, ending about 70 CE, with reuse in the Late Roman period and coffin burials of the fifth to seventh centuries CE.

text: Akeldama Cave 3, in the lower Ben Hinnom valley at the foot of the west bank of the Kidron valley, beside Cave 1 and probably cut before it. A rock-cut burial cave of four chambers: a main chamber and a lower chamber with loculi (kokhim), an elaborate passage chamber with three arcosolia and shallow burial troughs with headrests, and a back chamber used as an ossuary repository. The cave was entered through an opening in the upper part of the southeast wall of the main chamber, blocked by a square stone. The loculi had frames for sealing slabs; two shorter loculi probably served as repositories. The passage chamber is closed by two pivoting stone doors carved with panels. Its walls carry incised designs painted red, relief pilasters with pseudo-Doric capitals in the four corners of the chamber, and friezes. Sixteen ossuaries, twelve of them inscribed. Ossuary inscriptions give the names Hannah, Auge daughter of Do[ras], Erous, Kyria, Helene, Salome and Shelamzion daughters of Ariston, Shelamzion, Ariston of Apamea, Judah the proselyte, Shabtai son of Nehemiah, and Natira. The report dates the tomb's original burials to the first century CE, probably ending in 70 CE, with cremation burials of the Late Roman period.
